hits.text:
holy sh*t. Jev Founder, Diogo Almeida just released a 12-page PDF how turned Jev into a second brain for AI agents

a CLI for your Obsidian vault, a Claude Code plugin and a research paper. this is a 9-step blueprint on how to give your agents memory without paying an LLM to decide what's worth remembering:

step 1 → split the work: Jev decides what to remember, code applies the rules, the LLM only writes the note or the answer

step 2 → gate every capture with one call: save, todo, skip or review, plus is it private and how useful will it be in 30 days

step 3 → keep only what clears the bar: save at value 1.5+ and confidence 0.6+, anything private never leaves your machine

step 4 → let the LLM write one note, 5 to 12 lines, one claim. Jev never writes the body, or you end up with lossy compaction

step 5 → link it: Jev compares the new note with its neighbors and answers duplicate, related, revises or contradicts. related at 0.7+ gets wikilinks both ways

step 6 → read cheap, then judge: BM25 or embeddings pull the top 10 to 20, Jev keeps only what the question needs, 5 notes max go into context

step 7 → clean up every night: duplicates get a merge proposal, old notes get superseded_by, contradictions get a conflict stub, and you keep or reject

step 8 → don't build from zero: jev-second-brain runs on your vault, jevmem plugs into Claude Code, Jev-Mem is the paper if you're building agent memory yourself

step 9 → check the receipts: jevmem hit 98.5% on save/skip at 0.30s while six frontier LLMs took 2.8 to 4.3s, and Jev-Mem scored 0.777 vs 0.700 on LoCoMo with memory built 6.6x faster

your agent doesn't forget because the model is weak. it forgets because nothing ever decided what was worth keeping

memory was never a storage problem. it's a decision problem, and decisions are exactly what Jev is built for

stop giving your agent a bigger context window. give it a judge

Everyone is keeping quiet about this for now, but it's something everyone will be using soon

Claude + Jev = Second Brain

Diogo Almeida, who developed the Jev system, shared a simple thought "The point of Jev isn't to make the model smarter in a conversational sense, but to make it completely deterministic at decision points. If you have a choice of N actions, the system should yield an exact choice without hallucinations or wasted tokens"

Action Plan: 

Jev decides what to keep, code enforces the established rules, and the language model is left strictly with writing the final note or answer

At every input, Jev instantly determines its fate: save, set as a todo, skip, or flag for review, while evaluating privacy and its usefulness 30 days out

Filter only allows data through if it crosses the threshold for value and confidence, keeping all private details strictly local on your device

Instructs the model to generate a concise note of 5 to 12 lines focused on a single claim, prohibiting it from rewriting the core body to avoid lossy compaction

Compares the new note against its neighbors, detecting duplicates, relationships, or contradictions, and automatically sets bidirectional links for highly relevant notes

Pulls 10 to 20 candidates via BM25 or embeddings, then selects no more than 5 of the most precise notes to feed into the context window

Runs a nightly cleanup by proposing duplicate merges, flagging outdated entries, and pinpointing conflicts, leaving the final call to you

Integrates without building from scratch, running on your Obsidian vault, plugging into Claude Code, or acting as a ready-made memory framework

Delivers decisions with 98.5% accuracy in just 0.30s, outperforming major frontier models and building memory 6.6x faster

Your agent isn't forgetting because the model is weak; it forgets because nothing was deciding what was worth keeping in the first place

hits.text:
A student built a research model that answers in seconds what other models spend hours grinding through.

Nothing gets worked out from scratch. Your question is measured against every approach that already collapsed, and placed on that map.

> COLLECT - failed runs and dead-end attempts gathered instead of published results
> STRIP - each one cut down to the approach taken, with the write-up thrown away
> PATTERN - approaches that keep collapsing grouped across unrelated domains
> CROSS - groups checked against fields that never reference one another
> SCORE - a fresh question placed on that map before any compute is spent

Reasoning models start from zero on every prompt, however many times that exact wall has already been met.

The hours disappear there. Not into thought, but into walking back to an edge somebody mapped long ago.

An edge tells you the limits of a whole region. A win tells you about one spot, which is a far thinner piece of knowledge.

Some groups reach across domains. A method that dies in one discipline reappears wrecking something in another.

Speed is the whole story here. What used to be a long reasoning run is now the time it takes to paste a question in.

Nothing trains on what went wrong, because almost nobody records it in the first place.

The grouping method and the sharpest collapse patterns are laid out below.
